name: Harar Oromo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Owens, Jonathan. 1985. A Grammar of Harar Oromo (Northeastern Ethiopia). Kuschitische Sprachstudien / Cushitic Language Studies 4. Hamburg: Helmut Buske Verlag.
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'Tone': opening paragraph and 2.1 'Basic tone' (p. 26); 2.2 'Predictability of basic tone', points 1-2 (pp. 29-30). Rosetta Project excerpt archive.org id ('Oromo, Eastern Phonology', 11 pp.), pp. 7 and 10-11; page numbers are cropped in the scan, ch. 2 = p. 26 per the saved table of contents.
catalog_quote: Harar Oromo, like Booran, has a tone system which consists of three main parts: a classification of roots and affixes in terms of basic tone; a specification of the contexts where these basic tones may/must occur; and rules altering the tone on certain morphemes in certain contexts. ... I should note that I have found no lexical minimal pairs distinguished by tone alone in Harar Oromo. 2.1 Basic tone. All nominals (= nouns and non-phrasal noun modifiers) have a basic tone. This basic tone can be identified as the basic tone on the penultimate vowel of the word. ... [2.2] 1. First of all, only the penultimate or final syllable of a root can have a high tone, and all nominals except a few pronouns, demonstratives, and numerals (2.1.1) have at least one high tone. Moreover, if the penultimate is high-toned, the final must also be high. It is for this reason that only the penultimate syllable (the syllable before the final consonant) needs to have its tone marked in underlying form -- if it is high, then the following syllable must be high; if it is low, then the final syllable must be high. ... It will be clear from the preceding that although the possible basic tone patterns for nominals and affixes are quite limited, for the most part one cannot treat them as entirely predictable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Harar (Eastern) Oromo is described with two tones (H, L) but no lexical minimal pairs; prominence (H) in nominals is confined to a two-syllable window at the right edge: a nominal is either H on penult+final (HH) or H on the final only (…LH), the choice being partly lexical and partly predictable from shape (CVCa with short -a and most -aa-final nouns are LH/final-H; nouns ending in a long non-low vowel mostly have H penult; most long-vowel suffixes put H on the preceding syllable; an H that would become antepenultimate after suffixation shifts right). Verbs are inherently low-toned and get fixed H only from particular inflections (jussive H on first syllable, negative imperative H on penult). Nominal tone further alternates by syntactic context (basic tone vs all-low vs predicate-nominal pattern). de Lacy (2002: 124-5) restates the same nominal facts as stress: penultimate by default, final when the last vowel is a(:), quantity-insensitive, with H docking on the stressed syllable and spreading rightward.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; Owens notes only that a nominal may surface with two adjacent H syllables (penult+final), which he treats as one basic tone plus spreading rather than two prominences.
new_statements.exceptions: A few pronouns, demonstratives, numerals and possessives are all-low (no H); invariable adjectives ending in a long vowel have low penult / final H (adíi 'white', guutúu 'full', but k'ulk'úllúu, fagóo); four suffixes (-aa verbal noun, -aa participial, -uu concurrent, nominative) do not induce H on the preceding syllable; loans follow the same patterns (kúrsii 'chair', makiináa 'car'); in non-'basic-tone' syntactic contexts nominals can be entirely low-toned.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns the word-level 'basic tone' of nominals in citation/absolutive form (operationally: the noun as object of an imperative); Owens stresses that surface tone is also syntactically conditioned (2.3: basic tone vs all-low vs predicate-nominal contexts). Final short vowels get a glottal stop before pause and H-toned short vowels are phonetically longer (ch. 1, p. 10-11). Whether to call the system tone, pitch accent or stress is analyst-dependent: Owens (per Al Solami 2021, citing pp. 35-37) says pitch accent underlyingly, tone on the surface; de Lacy 2002 says stress with predictable H; Al Solami 2021 says restricted, stress-like tone system.
new_statements.identity_note: Owens 1985 describes the Oromo spoken in and around Harar city (Hararghe), 'Northeastern Ethiopia' in his title = Eastern Oromo [hae], Glottolog east2652; exact match to the target. Owens explicitly contrasts it with Booran (Southern Oromo, sout2649-area varieties) and Arussi. Al Solami 2021's consultant is also a Harar Oromo speaker. Habte Bulti 2003 (also saved) is on Macha = Western/West-Central Oromo (gaz, west2721) and was not used.

sources.citation: Al Solami, Majed. 2021. The Prosody of Harar Oromo Nouns. Jurnal Arbitrer 8(2): 107-130. doi:10.25077/ar.8.2.107-130.2021
sources.note: Acoustic (pitch-track) study of nouns with a Harar Oromo consultant. Reviews Owens 1985 (basic tone on penult, pp. 26-29; pitch accent underlyingly / tone on surface, pp. 35-37) and de Lacy 2002 (stress: penult by default, final if final vowel is [a(:)]). Own conclusion: noun roots are lexically accented (surface H) or accentless (L); nominative/accusative case suffixes always carry H in citation forms; lexical accent, when present, sits on the penultimate syllable of the stem; Harar Oromo has 'a restricted tone system that is more stress-like' (obligatoriness satisfied on the surface, culmin…

sources.note: Second-hand summary of Owens 1985: 26-30: Oromo nouns have an underlying H on the ultimate, or penultimate and ultimate, syllable ('Oromo's tone window is only two syllables'); most long-vowel suffixes impose H on the preceding syllable; treats the final-oriented H as a stress-like feature of Cushitic.
